notes.general_comments: If a single answer is asked for, two (or three) answers should not be given as incorrect statements may contradict correct answers. Candidates should ensure that at A level, numerical answers reflect the appropriate number of significant figures. Usually, most numerical answers, if not indicated otherwise, should be to three significant figures. Comments on specific questions
notes.1a: Most candidates secured this mark, but candidates should be advised to identify the toxic gas as NO rather than state the generic ‘toxic gas formed’, for example.
notes.1b: Most candidates are familiar with the reasoning behind weighing by difference and correct responses based upon the idea of needing to know the exact mass of brass transferred into flask A were frequently seen. Many candidates gave responses such as ‘so we know the mass of brass left in the beaker’ without going on to state the relevance of this mass. Weaker candidates assumed weighing by difference was done to ensure all the brass was transferred.
notes.1c: Nearly all candidates identified the apparatus needed as a volumetric pipette. The volume was not required for this particular question although there may be times when it will be. Candidates should be advised that burettes are not suitable for transfer of known volumes of solutions.
notes.1d: Nearly all candidates knew that the burette should be rinsed with the (0.0600 mol dm–3) aqueous sodium thiosulfate.
notes.1e: Despite this type of question frequently appearing in papers, many candidates struggled to describe the preparation of a standard solution from an aqueous solution. Most candidates correctly calculated the volume of 0.200 mol dm–3 Na S O (aq) as 30 cm3 but 2 2 3 omitted to give this as an accurate volumetric quantity of 30.00 cm3. A sizeable number of candidates did not appreciate that 30.00 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm–3 Na S O (aq) 2 2 3 can be placed directly into a 100 cm3 volumetric flask from a burette and opted to use a beaker as Many candidates insisted on rinsing the burette after addition of 30.00 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm–3 Na S O (aq) and adding the rinsings to the volumetric flask. This would have placed a greater 2 2 3 volume of 0.200 mol dm–3 Na S O (aq) into the volumetric flask. 2 2 3 Candidates should be advised that once the volumetric flask has been topped up to the 100 cm3 mark with distilled water, the flask should be stoppered and inverted several times.
notes.1f: Whilst the majority of candidates correctly gave the mass of brass added (1.00 g) using a two decimal place balance to two decimal places, some gave this mass to only one decimal place and others to a whole number of grams. Weaker candidates got this simple calculation wrong.

notes.1gii: /(iii) titres when calculating the mean titre in 1(g)(ii). Although percentage error calculation in 1(g)(iii) was better answered than in previous series, many candidates did not secure this mark. Half a burette graduation is 0.05 cm3 and two burette readings had to be made to produce a titre value of 22.40 cm3. This should have been taken into consideration for the percentage error calculation.
notes.1h: (i)-(v) This 5-part question was done very well by most candidates. Parts (i) to (iii) proved no problem but many did not scale up by a factor of 10 in part (iv). Even so, with an error carried forward mark, most provided a creditworthy answer to part (v), though many did not give their answer to three significant figures.
notes.2a: (i) It is concerning that candidates are not familiar with typical A level practical techniques such as refluxing. Many candidates could not draw a reflux condenser and label the flow of cold water correctly. Although detailed technical aspects of apparatus are not required, the diagrams should be good enough to show that the apparatus works.
notes.2aii: Although many candidates did gain credit here, a significant minority were unable to give the required answer of anti-bumping granules.
notes.2b: Most candidates realised that the suitable indicator was thymolphthalein, but very few could satisfactorily explain why. Very few candidates realised that potassium hydroxide is a strong alkali and, as it is used up in the reaction, the pH would fall from about 14 to 7 as equimolar amounts were used in the reaction and thymolphthalein was the only one of the three indicators which would change colour over this range.
notes.2c: The question asked candidates to ‘State what feature of the chromatogram …’. Many candidates did not refer to the chromatogram at all. There needed to be some reference to the spots or their R values. For example, ‘one of the spots in the reaction mixture had the same R value as the ester spot’. The common error was referring to the ‘extra’ spot for the reaction mixture.
notes.2d: This question was answered correctly by the majority of candidates as fractional distillation was known to most candidates.
notes.2e: The analysis of the infrared spectrum of ROH was done well by the majority of the candidates and a considerable number correctly identified the lack of a peak between 1710–1750 cm-1.
notes.2f: Very few candidates scored all 3 marks for this question. More could explain the singlet as coming from the proton in an –OH group in an alcohol than could explain the multiplet, which was from the However, even without scoring the first two marks for analysis of the (1H) spectrum, many candidates were able to identify the alcohol as propan–2–ol.
notes.2g: Most candidates could draw the ester group correctly and a pleasing number drew the complete displayed formula correctly. Candidates should be advised that a methyl group drawn as –CH is not a displayed formula. A significant minority misread the question and drew the displayed structure of the alcohol identified in 2(f).
notes.2h: Very few candidates noticed the fact that concentrated sulfuric acid was a catalyst and therefore the pH of the mixture would not (significantly) change. Thus, none of the indicators would change colour.
